title: Benjamin Franklin invented an instrument that Mozart and Beethoven wrote music for

cover.alt: A reproduction glass armonica in a museum case: a row of graduated glass bowls on a horizontal rod, set in an open wooden case on a desk-like stand, with a sheet of music propped behind.

body: In May 1761 Benjamin Franklin watched Edward Delaval play water-filled wine glasses in Cambridge, England, and set out to build a mechanical version. His glass armonica, named after the Italian word for harmony, mounted glass bowls side by side on an iron spindle that the player turned with a foot pedal, touching the spinning rims with moistened fingers to make them sing. Franklin wrote that its tones were ‘incomparably sweet beyond those of any other’, and it caught the ear of great composers: **Mozart** wrote two pieces for it in 1791, and **Beethoven** used it in 1814.

slides.question: How many glass bowls were mounted on the spindle of Franklin’s pedal-driven armonica?
slides.explanation: 37 bowls, mounted horizontally on an iron spindle and turned by a foot pedal.

steps.label: A foot pedal spins a rod of glass bowls
Fingers touch the rims as they turn
Each bowl rings with its own note

events.text: Mozart writes K. 617 and K. 356 for it
Beethoven uses it in Leonore Prohaska
Glassblower Gerhard Finkenbeiner revives the design

left.label: Rumour
left.text: The armonica drove players and listeners mad, or poisoned players through its lead glass.

right.label: Evidence
right.text: The madness tales seem mostly German, and their spread is guesswork. Simply touching lead glass has no known link to lead poisoning.

slides.question: Gerhard Finkenbeiner’s firm still makes armonicas. What are their bowls made of?
slides.explanation: Fused-silica quartz. Finkenbeiner reworked Franklin’s design in 1984, and his firm in Waltham, Massachusetts, carries on.
